Informed Patient consent to permit the receipt, processing and release of data by the HSCIC

texts.69d4699d9e9b: The Data Recipient agrees to process the Data only for the following purposes agreed with the HSCIC: Objective for processing: The 13-ACS-22: National Elective Revascularisation PROMS Pilot was initially a Department of Health project, passed onto NHS England in April 2013, for which the National Cardiac Benchmarking Collaborative (NCBC) (which is itself comprised of 28 NHS and Foundation Trusts and run by Miles-Green Associates Ltd) and the Liverpool Heart & Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust have been contracted to undertake analysis and evaluation. The purposes of the pilot are: 1. To determine the feasibility of routinely collecting patient reported outcome measures (PROMs) in patients receiving coronary revascularisation. 2. To explore the usefulness of these measures to clinicians as aids to improving the quality of revascularisation services. 3. To report findings to NHS England for consideration of the suitability of mandatory collection of these data by provider Trusts, informing the NHS Outcomes Framework. The data provided by HSCIC will be used solely for the purposes above, and specifically not used for any commercial purpose. No patient record level data will be provided to any third party; analyses with small numbers will be suppressed. Miles-Green Associates Ltd working as the National Cardiac Benchmarking Collaborative (NCBC) have an long-established track record in providing a comprehensive analytical services to NHS organisations and producing innovative feedback of clinical data which is then used by clinical teams to improve local clinical practice, fostering collaboration and service improvement. They also have a long track-record of working on user/patient-surveys, and wider population based research and health needs assessment. Liverpool Heart & Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust has been a member of the NCBC since its inception (2006)); Dr Jackson sits on the NCBC National Steering Group. Processing activities: There are three distinct datasets being used in this pilot: 1. The National Institute for Cardiovascular Outcomes Research (NICOR) record resulting from the submission of a national clinical audit dataset by each provider that contains the clinical details of the index revascularisation procedure (the NICOR record). 2. The Patient Reported Outcomes Measure (PROMs) record resulting from the electronic transcription of questionnaires completed by the patients before and after their revascularisation procedure (the PROMS record). 3. The Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) record covering the index revascularisation procedure (the HES record). The PROMS and HES records are already linked, and held by both the Liverpool Heart & Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and Miles-Green Associates Ltd. In support of this, the following data flows will be established: 1. NICOR/CCAD will send patient identifiers (NHS Number, Date of Birth, Gender, local Hospital Number) plus the admission date of the revascularisation operation and Study ID to the HSCIC under the auspices of the Section 251 (ref ECC-1-06(d)/2011); policy available at http://www.ucl.ac.uk/nicor/access/application) for all the people in their Society for Cardiothoracic Surgery (SCTS) and British Cardiovascular Intervention Society (BCIS) data bases who are recorded as having had an (elective) revascularisation procedure in the 11 NCBC Trusts participating in the Pilot during the period covered by PROMS pilot, with appropriate follow up to catch procedures performed very late (November 2011 to April 2014 for the maximum match rate. 2. HSCIC via the cohort will identify and extract the patients who completed a PROMS Q1. 3. HSCIC will send back to NICOR/CCAD the list of patients who completed PROMS Q1er’s. This list will comprise of the matching Study ID’s for those patients to reduce the flow of patient identifiable information. 4. NICOR will use the Study ID to locate and match and send back to HSCIC the clinical data for this subset of the original NICOR/CCAD provided list of patients. 5. HSCIC will link the NICOR/CCAD clinical records to the PROMS serial numbers 6. HSCIC will transfer (via SEFT) the linked pseudonymised-sensitive data (the clinical data from NICOR/CCAD, and PROMS serial number) to Liverpool Heart & Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and Miles-Green Associates ltd. Liverpool Heart & Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust together with Miles-Green Associates Ltd will then undertake in depth analysis to determine: • Recruitment and percentage of the response rates to the questionnaires • The practical and logistical implications of undertaking national PROMS in this group of patients and general issues arising from the pilot • Possible reasons for different recruitment and response rates • The health gain/loss associated with each of the different revascularisation procedures • The association of health gain/ loss with demographic and clinical variables (e.g. extent of revascularisation, quality of left ventricular function, previous cardiac history in order to identify whether it is possible to predict which types of patients benefit most from the revascularisation procedure. The extent to which preoperative health status influences final outcomes characterised by size of health gain (or loss). Specific outputs expected, including target date(s): Outputs from the analyses will be fed back to the PROMS steering group in the first instance (iteratively until December 2015) before being presented at the National Collaborative Benchmarking Collaborative NCBC 2015/16 Annual conference (early 2016). A report for NHS England that addresses the purposes described above (September- December 2015). A number of presentations and national and international conferences together with publications in academic cardiology journals that describe the detail of this experience and the quality improvement opportunities resulting from it (2016/17/18). All outputs will be in aggregate non-identifiable form. Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care, including target date(s): Specifically, The customer expects this work to help identify: 1. Those subgroups of patients who may not benefit from a revascularisation procedure, including those who may die prematurely enabling clinicians to better be able to assess suitability, and potential benefits for revascularisation. 2. Those subgroups of patients who may benefit substantially, enabling patients with similar characteristics to be more easily identified for future revascularisation procedures. 3. The clinical factors that may be associated with more successful outcomes, so that future patients can be optimised before their procedure, to improve resultant benefits. 4. Whether patient reported outcome measures for these interventions are a useful complement to other routine clinical measures for the assessment of hospital and clinical team quality and performance. Whether these new measures and the information gathered from patients about their measured outcomes could help improve decision-making for other patients and families and their clinical advisers when faced with the prospect of invasive cardiac treatment for their heart condition.

Objective for processing: 
The 13-ACS-22: National Elective Revascularisation PROMS Pilot was initially a Department of Health project, passed onto NHS England in April 2013, for which the National Cardiac Benchmarking Collaborative (NCBC) (which is itself comprised of 28 NHS and Foundation Trusts and run by Miles-Green Associates Ltd) and the Liverpool Heart & Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust have been contracted to undertake analysis and evaluation.
The purposes of the pilot are:
1. To determine the feasibility of routinely collecting patient reported outcome measures (PROMs) in patients receiving coronary revascularisation.
2. To explore the usefulness of these measures to clinicians as aids to improving the quality of revascularisation services.
3. To report findings to NHS England for consideration of the suitability of mandatory collection of these data by provider Trusts, informing the NHS Outcomes Framework.
The data provided by HSCIC will be used solely for the purposes above, and specifically not used for any commercial purpose.
No patient record level data will be provided to any third party; analyses with small numbers will be suppressed.  
Miles-Green Associates Ltd working as the National Cardiac Benchmarking Collaborative (NCBC) have an long-established track record in providing a comprehensive analytical services to NHS organisations and producing innovative feedback of clinical data which is then used by clinical teams to improve local clinical practice, fostering collaboration and service improvement. They also have a long track-record of working on user/patient-surveys, and wider population based research and health needs assessment. 
Liverpool Heart & Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust has been a member of the NCBC since its inception (2006)); Dr Jackson sits on the NCBC National Steering Group.

Processing activities: 
There are three distinct datasets being used in this pilot:
1.	The National Institute for Cardiovascular Outcomes Research (NICOR) record resulting from the submission of a national clinical audit dataset by each provider that contains the clinical details of the index revascularisation procedure (the NICOR record).
2.	The Patient Reported Outcomes Measure (PROMs) record resulting from the electronic transcription of questionnaires completed by the patients before and after their revascularisation procedure (the PROMS record).
3.	The Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) record covering the index revascularisation procedure (the HES record).
The PROMS and HES records are already linked, and held by both the Liverpool Heart & Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and Miles-Green Associates Ltd. 
In support of this, the following data flows will be established:
1.	NICOR/CCAD will send patient identifiers (NHS Number, Date of Birth, Gender, local Hospital Number) plus the admission date of the revascularisation operation and Study ID to the HSCIC under the auspices of  the Section 251 (ref ECC-1-06(d)/2011); policy available at http://www.ucl.ac.uk/nicor/access/application) for all the people in their Society for Cardiothoracic Surgery (SCTS) and British Cardiovascular Intervention Society (BCIS) data bases who are recorded as having had an (elective) revascularisation procedure in the 11 NCBC Trusts participating in the Pilot during the period covered by PROMS pilot, with appropriate follow up to catch procedures performed very late (November 2011 to April 2014 for the maximum match rate.
2.	HSCIC via the cohort will identify and extract the patients who completed a PROMS Q1.
3.	HSCIC will send back to NICOR/CCAD the list of patients who completed PROMS Q1er’s. This list will comprise of the matching Study ID’s for those patients to reduce the flow of patient identifiable information.
4.	NICOR will use the Study ID to locate and match and send back to HSCIC the clinical data for this subset of the original NICOR/CCAD provided list of patients.
5.	HSCIC will link the NICOR/CCAD clinical records to the PROMS serial numbers 
6.	HSCIC will transfer (via SEFT) the linked pseudonymised-sensitive data (the clinical data from NICOR/CCAD, and PROMS serial number) to Liverpool Heart & Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and Miles-Green Associates ltd.
Liverpool Heart & Chest Hospital NHS Foundation Trust together with Miles-Green Associates Ltd will then undertake  in depth analysis to determine:
•	Recruitment and percentage of the response rates to the questionnaires
•	The practical and logistical implications of undertaking national PROMS in this group of patients and general issues arising from the pilot
•	Possible reasons for different recruitment and response rates
•	The health gain/loss associated with each of the different revascularisation procedures
•	The association of health gain/ loss with demographic and clinical variables (e.g. extent of revascularisation, quality of left ventricular function, previous cardiac history in order to identify whether it is possible to predict which types of patients benefit most from the revascularisation procedure. 
The extent to which preoperative health status influences final outcomes characterised by size of health gain (or loss).

Specific outputs expected, including target date(s): 
Outputs from the analyses will be fed back to the PROMS steering group in the first instance (iteratively until December 2015) before being presented at the National Collaborative Benchmarking Collaborative NCBC 2015/16 Annual conference (early 2016).
A report for NHS England that addresses the purposes described above (September- December 2015).
A number of presentations and national and international conferences together with publications in academic cardiology journals that describe the detail of this experience and the quality improvement opportunities resulting from it (2016/17/18).
All outputs will be in aggregate non-identifiable form.
Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care, including target date(s): 
Specifically, The customer expects this work to help identify:
1.	Those subgroups of patients who may not benefit from a revascularisation procedure, including those who may die prematurely enabling clinicians to better be able to assess suitability, and potential benefits for revascularisation.
2.	Those subgroups of patients who may benefit substantially, enabling patients with similar characteristics to be more easily identified for future revascularisation procedures.
3.	The clinical factors that may be associated with more successful outcomes, so that future patients can be optimised before their procedure, to improve resultant benefits. 
4.	Whether patient reported outcome measures for these interventions are a useful complement to other routine clinical measures for the assessment of hospital and clinical team quality and performance.
Whether these new measures and the information gathered from patients about their measured outcomes could help improve decision-making for other patients and families and their clinical advisers when faced with the prospect of invasive cardiac treatment for their heart condition.
